data: FBX vs GLB: which 3D format is best for games?
FBX is Autodesk's interchange format; GLB is the binary form of the open glTF standard. How they differ on materials, animation, size and engine support.
AssetHoard, the local-first asset manager for indie game developers

Neither is better everywhere. GLB is an open standard with consistent PBR materials, a single self-contained file and built-in compression options, which makes it the better choice for Godot, the web and sharing models. FBX is better supported by older tools and long-established Unity and Unreal pipelines, especially for complex character animation. For a new project, GLB is usually the safer default unless your tools or engine expect FBX.
What is the difference between FBX and GLB?

FBX is a proprietary format owned by Autodesk, with no public specification. GLB is the binary form of glTF 2.0, an open, royalty-free standard from the Khronos Group. GLB packs the mesh, PBR materials, textures and animation into one file and uses fixed units and axes, while FBX materials and scale often come out differently depending on the program that exported them.
Not out of the box. Unity imports FBX natively, and glTF and GLB support comes from a package such as Unity's glTFast, which you add through the Package Manager.
Yes. Godot 4.3 and later import FBX files natively. Godot still recommends glTF as its preferred 3D format, and earlier Godot 4 versions needed the external FBX2glTF tool to import FBX.
How do I convert FBX to GLB?

The simplest free way is Blender. Choose File, Import, FBX, check the model looks right, then choose File, Export, glTF 2.0 and pick the glTF Binary (.glb) format. Check the materials after converting, because FBX materials do not always map cleanly to glTF's PBR model.
What is the difference between GLB and glTF?

They are the same format in two packagings. A .gltf file is JSON that usually points at a separate .bin file of geometry and separate image files for textures. A .glb packs all of that into one binary file, which is easier to share and load.

FBX is Autodesk's proprietary 3D interchange format, the long-standing default for moving animated models between modelling tools and game engines. GLB is the binary form of glTF 2.0, an open standard from the Khronos Group built for delivering 3D at runtime, with the mesh, PBR materials, textures and animation packed into one file. The short answer: use GLB for Godot, the web, and sharing or archiving models, and FBX when your engine or animation pipeline expects it, which still often means Unity and Unreal character work.

The rest of this post goes through the differences that actually matter for game development.

FBX vs GLB at a glance

FBX GLB (glTF 2.0)
Owner Autodesk Khronos Group, open standard
Specification Not public, read through Autodesk's SDK Public and royalty-free
Files One .fbx, textures often separate One .glb with textures embedded
Materials Older material model, PBR varies by exporter Metallic-roughness PBR built in
Units and axes Vary by exporting program Always metres, Y up
Animation Skeletal, blend shapes, very mature Skeletal, morph targets, multiple clips
Compression None standard Draco or meshopt meshes, KTX2 textures
Unity Native Through a package such as glTFast
Unreal Engine Native Built-in importer in Unreal Engine 5
Godot Native since Godot 4.3 Native, the recommended format
Web (three.js, Babylon.js) Limited The standard

Materials

This is the difference you are most likely to notice. glTF defines a single metallic-roughness PBR material model, so a GLB exported from Blender should look the same in Godot, three.js or any other glTF viewer. Base colour, metallic, roughness, normal, occlusion and emissive maps all have a defined place.

FBX predates modern PBR. Its core material properties come from older lighting models, and each program fills in PBR values its own way. That is why an FBX that looks right in one tool often arrives in an engine with flat colours, missing roughness, or textures that need reconnecting by hand.

If texture maps are your pain point, our explainer on what an ORM texture is covers how glTF packs occlusion, roughness and metallic into one image.

Scale and orientation

glTF fixes its units as metres and its up axis as Y. FBX stores units and axes as settings, and different programs choose differently. The classic symptom is a model that imports at 100 times its intended size, or lying on its back. Most engines have import options to correct this, but with GLB there is nothing to correct.

Animation

Both formats handle skeletal animation, blend shapes (called morph targets in glTF) and multiple animation clips in one file. FBX has decades of tooling behind it for complex rigs, and services such as Mixamo export FBX, so it remains the default in many character pipelines. glTF animation is solid for most game use, and exporters have caught up a lot.

File size

A GLB packs everything into one binary file, and glTF supports Draco and meshopt mesh compression and KTX2 GPU-compressed textures. Compressed, a GLB is often a fraction of the size of the equivalent FBX, which matters for web games, downloads and large libraries. Our free GLB compressor shrinks a GLB in the browser, and the mesh reducer cuts the polygon count.

Engine support

  • Unity imports FBX natively. GLB and glTF need a package such as Unity's glTFast, added through the Package Manager.
  • Unreal Engine imports FBX natively, and Unreal Engine 5 has a built-in glTF importer.
  • Godot treats glTF as its preferred format. Godot 4.3 and later also import FBX natively, while earlier Godot 4 versions needed the external FBX2glTF tool.
  • Blender imports and exports both.
  • Web engines such as three.js and Babylon.js are built around glTF.

When to use FBX

  • Your engine is Unity and you do not want to add a glTF package.
  • You are working with an existing Maya, 3ds Max or MotionBuilder pipeline, or a service such as Mixamo that outputs FBX.
  • The asset pack you bought only ships FBX. Many Asset Store packs do.

When to use GLB

  • You use Godot, or you are building for the web.
  • You want a model to look the same everywhere, with PBR materials that survive the trip.
  • You want one self-contained file to share, sell or archive.
  • File size matters, and you want mesh and texture compression.

How to convert FBX to GLB

The free route is Blender:

  1. File, Import, FBX, then check the model, its scale and its materials.
  2. Fix anything that came in wrong, usually texture connections or roughness values.
  3. File, Export, glTF 2.0, and choose glTF Binary (.glb) as the format.

Then open the result in our free glTF viewer or model inspector to check it looks the way you expect. For OBJ files, our OBJ to GLB converter does the job in the browser.

Keeping both formats in one library

Most game devs end up with both. Asset Store packs come as FBX, free CC0 packs often come as GLB or glTF, and older packs as OBJ. AssetHoard previews FBX, glTF, GLB, OBJ and more side by side, renders a thumbnail for every model on import, and lets you orbit any of them in an interactive viewer, so you can find a model by sight whatever format it is in. See AssetHoard for 3D game devs and artists or the 3D files documentation.

What is a .uasset file? Unreal packages explained
A .uasset is Unreal Engine's binary package format, holding one asset such as a mesh or texture. What is inside, and how to open one outside Unreal.
AssetHoard showing Unreal Engine .uasset packages from a project, with 3D model thumbnails for static and skeletal meshes and bundles for audio, levels, materials, models and sprites

A .uasset is Unreal Engine's package format. It is a binary file that holds one asset, such as a static mesh, texture, material, sound or Blueprint, together with a header listing the other packages it depends on. Every asset in an Unreal project's Content folder is stored as a .uasset, apart from levels, which use .umap.
How do I open a .uasset file?

Copy it into the Content folder of an Unreal project made with the same or a newer engine version, keeping its folder structure, and it appears in the Content Browser. To move assets between projects with their dependencies, use the editor's Migrate option rather than copying files by hand. To browse and preview .uasset files without opening the editor, use a tool that reads the format directly, such as AssetHoard.
Can I open a .uasset in an older version of Unreal Engine?
No. An asset saved in a newer engine version cannot be loaded by an older one. Assets from older versions do open in newer versions, and are upgraded when you save them.
What is the difference between .uasset and .umap?
Both use the same package format. A .umap holds a level, with the actors placed in it. A .uasset holds any other kind of asset, such as a mesh, texture, material, sound or Blueprint.

When Unreal cooks a game for release, it can split each package in two. The .uasset keeps the header, and the .uexp holds the serialised object data. Large data such as texture mips can go into a third .ubulk file. Packages in an editor project's Content folder are normally a single .uasset.
Can I convert a .uasset to FBX?

Not directly, because a .uasset is Unreal's own format. Open the project in the Unreal Editor, right-click the mesh in the Content Browser, choose Asset Actions, then Export, and save it as FBX. Textures can be exported as image files the same way.

A .uasset file is Unreal Engine's package format: a binary file that holds one asset, such as a static mesh, texture, material, sound or Blueprint, along with a header listing everything that asset depends on. Every asset in an Unreal project's Content folder is a .uasset, apart from levels, which are .umap files in the same format. This post covers what is inside one, how .umap, .uexp and cooked packages differ, and how to open a .uasset with or without the Unreal Editor.

What is inside a .uasset file?

A .uasset is not a mesh file or an image file with a different extension. It is a container that Unreal serialises its own objects into, and it has a few parts:

  • A package summary with the engine version that saved it, flags and offsets to the rest of the file.
  • A name table of every name the package uses, so each one is stored only once.
  • An import table listing the objects this package depends on: classes from /Script/, engine content from /Engine/, and other assets in your project under /Game/.
  • An export table listing the objects this package defines, usually one main asset plus any sub-objects it owns.
  • The serialised object data, such as vertex buffers, texture mips or audio.
  • In editor packages, a thumbnail of the asset, which is what the Content Browser shows.

The import table is why moving .uasset files around in Windows Explorer or Finder breaks things. A material refers to its textures by /Game/ paths, so if the textures move without Unreal knowing, the references point at nothing.

.uasset, .umap, .uexp and .ubulk

Extension What it is
.uasset A package holding one asset: mesh, texture, material, sound, Blueprint, data table and so on
.umap A package holding a level, with the actors placed in it
.uexp In cooked builds, the object data split out of a .uasset, which keeps only the header
.ubulk In cooked builds, large bulk data such as texture mips, split out again
.pak, .utoc, .ucas Containers a shipped game packs its cooked packages into

Uncooked and cooked packages

The .uasset files in your project's Content folder are uncooked. They keep editor-only data such as thumbnails and source audio, and they are what the Unreal Editor loads.

When you package a game, Unreal cooks that content for the target platform: it strips editor-only data, converts textures and audio to platform formats, splits packages into .uasset and .uexp files, and usually seals the lot inside .pak or IoStore containers. Cooked packages are built to load fast in a game, not to be edited, so most tools that work with project content expect uncooked packages.

How to open a .uasset file in Unreal Engine

  • Use a project of the same or a newer engine version. An asset saved in a newer version of Unreal cannot be loaded by an older one. Older assets do open in newer versions, and are upgraded when you save them.
  • Copy it into the project's Content folder, keeping its folder structure. It appears in the Content Browser, and its /Game/ references resolve as long as the assets it depends on are where it expects them.
  • To move assets between projects, use Migrate. Right-click the asset in the Content Browser and choose Asset Actions, Migrate. Unreal copies the asset and everything it references into the other project's Content folder with the paths intact.
  • To get a mesh or texture out of Unreal, right-click it and choose Asset Actions, Export. Meshes export as FBX, textures as image files.

You cannot read a .uasset in a text editor or an image viewer, and there is no direct converter to FBX or PNG. The editor is the usual way in, which is slow when all you want is to see what a file is.

How to open a .uasset without the Unreal Editor

AssetHoard reads .uasset and .umap packages directly from disk. There is no editor to launch and no plugin to install in Unreal:

  • Packages are classified by what they contain. AssetHoard reads the main object in each package, so meshes show up as 3D models, PaperSprites and flipbooks as sprites, SoundWaves and SoundCues as audio, and textures and materials as themselves.
  • Previews are real. Static and skeletal meshes open in an interactive 3D viewer, flipbooks play at their real frame rate, and audio plays in place. Anything else shows the thumbnail Unreal baked into the package.
  • Dependencies are mapped. Every /Game/ reference is matched against your library, so you can see which textures a material uses and which are missing.
  • You can export with dependencies. Drag an asset out, or right-click and export it, and AssetHoard writes a Content-shaped folder with everything it references, ready to drop into another project.
  • Your project is never changed. AssetHoard only reads packages.

It fully parses uncooked packages from UE4.10 to UE5.5. Packages from UE5.6 and newer import as generic packages for now, and cooked packages classify and resolve references but fall back to an icon instead of a rich preview. The Unreal packages documentation has the details, and AssetHoard for Unreal Engine has the overview.

If you are still choosing an engine, our Unreal vs Unity comparison may help.

Artist spotlight: Christoph Kühl on building Life Altered
Solo developer Christoph Kühl on Life Altered, a dice-driven nature deckbuilder, and how he mixes commissions, asset packs and public domain scientific art on an indie budget.
A Life Altered battle in a rainy mangrove swamp: three heroes face a mutated Mangrove Root Crab while a Gorilla card is played from their dice

Welcome back to our Artist Spotlight series, where we chat with creators in the game dev space about their work, their process, and what they have learned along the way.

This time we are talking to Christoph Kühl, the solo developer behind Senescent Leaf. He is building Life Altered, a roguelike deckbuilder that stores its cards in dice, in the time between a day job and parenting. Along the way he has worked out an asset pipeline that mixes commissioned art, bought packs and centuries-old scientific illustrations.

For anyone who has not seen it yet, how would you describe Life Altered?

Life Altered is a nature based deckbuilder that blends dice and card gameplay. I'm guessing that both the "nature" and the "dice" part need explaining.

Let's get to the dice first. In any traditional deckbuilder you draw your cards from a deck and throw them on a discard pile after your turn ends. In Life Altered your cards are collected in and played through dice. So if your die lands on honey badger, you get to play the honey badger card. This opens up new gameplay and deck management strategies compared to the classic card-only mechanic.

And nature? Well, the cards are all of Earth's most interesting, weird and dangerous life forms. Bullet ant (inflicts pain), wombat (fights with its butt), ginkgo tree (grants more energy). It's been fun to research and implement all those creatures.

Story-wise it's about an alien virus that mutates all life on Earth except people who are gifted with magic-like animal and plant abilities, who try to fight their way through infected regions to find a cure.

The Life Altered trailer. There is more on Christoph's YouTube channel, including a playthrough by the developer himself.

Who is behind Senescent Leaf, and how did a biologist end up making games?

I love nature and science. It's the reason I studied biology at university. So when the time came to find a setting for my game, I naturally drifted to what I know.

I tried to reflect that in the studio's name. Leaf senescence is one of the first things that fascinated me about plant biology. It describes the process of leaves turning yellow and red in autumn. Being an early touchpoint of science in my life, it marks a beginning for me, but it is also about something ending, a leaf's life, only to be born again come spring. And I do enjoy a good metaphor for beginnings and endings. Being a game dev is a new beginning for me, after all.

Some people view science as separate from art; sometimes they even use the words as antonyms. But I don't see them as mutually exclusive. I have been trying to find a creative outlet pretty much my whole life. I tried writing, film making, drawing, making music, acting: nothing stuck. I have also been a gamer my whole life, but it never seemed like a realistic possibility to make games myself. The programming part scared me off, which turned out to be wrong, of course.

I finally tried the GameMaker engine and with my first game I feel like a fish in water. I love designing gameplay, I love coding it, I love animating the creatures. That is also what makes it alright if the game happens to fail commercially. Even if it never makes money, I'll have loved every minute of making it.

Do you make the assets yourself, work with other artists, or use bought or free packs?

Visual art is one of my limitations. I don't enjoy drawing and so I cannot bring myself to get better at it. So I use (mostly paid) asset packs where it's feasible, and there are great packs for UI, for example. Then I commission artists for anything too specific or important to come from an asset pack. There are no asset packs for mutated bilbies, snow leopards and dung beetles.

Finding an artist you can trust and afford, and whose quality matches your vision, is not easy, and in the age of AI it is more difficult still. I tried a couple of artists on Fiverr before I landed on someone I was happy to work with. Now all the enemies in the game are made by Riko Agustian P. My brief is usually short: "Give me a horribly mutated [insert animal] viewed from the front, in your own style." He delivers the illustrations and later I animate them myself. Fiverr can be shady and dangerous in many ways, but if you find an artist to partner with, it is a great way to handle image rights and payment.

I also found some artists through asset packs that looked good but didn't quite fit my game. I just contact the creator to ask if they work on commission too. That's how I found the Ukrainian studio Moon Tribe, who did my background environments, and Penzilla, who made icons for me.

And lastly, the actual animals and plants on the cards would be too many for me to afford on a commission basis. Luckily, there are wonderful public domain images from old scientific journals of all kinds of life forms. Looking through those archives is very much like digging for gold. When you find something good it's a great feeling.

The dice appear as an unfolded net rather than rolling in 3D. Was that a design choice from the start, or did a technical limit push you there?

I am actually still not sure I landed on the best way to depict the dice. I might like real 3D dice, but GameMaker is still a 2D-focused engine and it is really difficult to make 3D work. Even if I could figure that out, 3D dice might just look too goofy in an otherwise 2D setting. (It does look weird in Slice & Dice, for example, even though I love that game a lot.) So I spin my 2D dice in place to roll them, and show a foldout layout in the character screens.

Were there other moments where a constraint shaped how the game looks?

Generally, the limits of the UI have played a large role in shaping Life Altered's gameplay. For example, I originally wanted each character to have four dice instead of three. The only reason I didn't do that is that I couldn't fit 12 dice on the screen. Now I think it's for the best, because nine dice is the right number gameplay-wise. But I spent days trying to find a way to fit 12 on the screen.

Honey badgers, bullet ants, mantis shrimp, sequoia trees. How does one creature go from an idea to a finished in-game asset?

I start by researching plants and animals with interesting facts about them, like the tarantula hawk, which paralyses its prey and lays eggs inside it that later hatch and eat their host. I think about how that translates into a good card mechanic (stun the enemy and lay eggs, which hatch after three turns to do X damage) and code it.

For the card art it's a simple matter of looking for a suitable image of the species in the Biodiversity Heritage Library and cutting it to size for the cards and dice in Krita.

With up to three evolutions stacked on a creature, how do you show that visually?

The card is basically three layers on top of each other:

  1. Bottom layer: the species art
  2. Middle layer: the card frame, with a hole to show the species art
  3. Top layer: the evolution markers

I would love to show evolved species as new sprites, but I just can't afford to create the assets, so I am working with pip-style evolution markers.

What tools are in your art and audio pipeline, and how do those files get into the engine?

My main tools are Clip Studio Paint, Krita, Figma, Spine and AssetHoard.

My main artist uses Clip Studio Paint, which is lucky, since I bought a licence for it back when I tried my hand at digital drawing. That lets me check and edit his illustrations in the original source file.

Whenever he sends me a new enemy illustration, I start by separating the body parts I want to animate and exporting them as PNG files, so I can import them into Spine for animation.

Why Spine?

Spine is the most expensive software I have bought, but it's worth it. It is surprisingly easy to use once you have watched one or two tutorials, and I love the results I am getting. The process is basically:

  1. Import the body parts I cut out.
  2. Create a mesh for each body part.
  3. Add bones and bind them to the meshed body parts.
  4. Move the bones at key frames to create the animations. I mostly need idle, attack, hurt and death animations.

The whole thing takes four to six hours or so per enemy. I can then export the animated illustration as an atlas file, which GameMaker supports natively. The engine lets me control the animations with code.

Krita is open source software that I use as an alternative to Photoshop. I need it to adjust, resize or colour correct assets. Figma has been very useful for creating and adjusting UI elements.

Handy overlap: AssetHoard shows previews of Krita files and Clip Studio Paint files straight in the library, imports Spine exports with atlas thumbnails and skeleton details, and works with GameMaker projects too.

And audio?

I don't really use audio tools, except for Audacity to record some voice-over for promotional materials. I use audio files from asset packs that I import into GameMaker, and adjust their volume in-engine.

AssetHoard has been extremely helpful for finding and previewing audio files to use in my game. I apparently amassed 70,000 audio files through various Humble Bundles. Browsing through them with Windows Explorer would be virtually impossible.

70,000 is a lot of bundles. Here is how we keep 100,000 game assets findable.

What is one thing about making assets for a game this size that you wish you had known at the start?

I think the main thing I would do differently is put more thought into art direction before buying any assets or commissions and putting them in the game.

I spent a not insignificant amount of money on art that ultimately had no place in the game. The game started out as a pixel art project, for example, before I realised that I could not afford to do the whole game in that style.

I worked on the game for at least a year before I started methodically mocking up screens in Figma. Mock-ups are a quick and cheap way of figuring out which types of assets work well together and how they can be spaced on the screen. I wish that had been my process from the start.

What is left to do before launch, and is there a release window you can share?

There is still lots to do. Mainly three more characters with 40 cards each, ten more enemies, an ascension system and some story beats. I think I can release a demo in early 2027, and I hope to release the full game by the end of 2027.
